Faster software installation and setup
Reduced compatibility issues
Given the advancement of virtualization technologies, cloud vendors such as AWS can offer an
almost endless supply of virtual machines to the rest of the world, enabling businesses to build
highly available, scalable, and cost-effective solutions. This technology has undergone
substantial innovation, enabling AWS to offer its customers managed platforms and services,
as well as the concept of serverless architectures. We will discuss these more advanced
solutions in subsequent chapters.
To understand how cloud services differ, it helps to look at the main service models that define
how much idx_18cbd461 responsibility you keep and how much the idx_b0e38c0e cloud provider manages for you. In the
next section, you will learn about three different cloud computing service models, each
offering various levels of control, flexibility, and management.
Comparing cloud computing service models
Businesses require idx_21f3d763 a wide range of applications, and cloud computing offers the ability to
offload the cost and complexity associated with hosting and managing those applications.
Often, businesses will use a idx_f7650d52 combination of off-the-shelf (OTS) products and specific line-of-
business applications, some of which are designed and built in-house.
Cloud computing models offer a way to cater to all such variations. So, for example, many
cloud providers offer productivity suites as a complete end-to-end software package. Examples
include Microsoft Office 365, which offers a suite comprising word processing, spreadsheets,
presentation software, and desktop-level databases, among many others. At the same time,
businesses will often have special in-house developed or bespoke software solutions that must
be deployed on a custom-built infrastructure. A cloud provider, such as AWS, can provide
access to virtual infrastructure components comprising VMs, networks, storage, and
databases.
Cloud computing services can be offered across three separate models. The model you choose
for your project will depend on your application-specific needs and the level of control you
require of the underlying infrastructure that supports your application stack. The following
sections provide an overview of each of these model types.
Infrastructure as a service
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a idx_e687ac9c cloud computing model idx_81c817cc that delivers virtualized
components to enable you to build your cloud environments. These include compute, network,
and storage services offering maximum flexibility, allowing you to define custom-built cloud
networks with necessary security configurations. This model will enable you to deploy virtual

machines hosting various operating systems, applications, and storage services to host and
manage data. This model is closely related to traditional on-premises environments, except
that you do not have direct access to the underlying hardware and can only define
configuration items from the virtual idx_8bb0b0b0 machine's operating system (OS) layer upward.
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is an example idx_ece731c0 of IaaS. The service enables you to
deploy virtual machines (servers) running a choice of Linux, Microsoft, or MacOS operating
systems and comes in various configurations to support different use cases – capable of
hosting standard websites through idx_59a76528 more intensive high-performance computing (HPC)
applications.
Platform as a service
Platform as a Service (PaaS) is a cloud idx_df6c2d37 computing model idx_e0c29002 that enables you to focus more on
your application code and its development lifecycle rather than spend time and effort
configuring underlying infrastructure resources. This is because when you supply your
application code, you also provide details such as the language and framework used to build
the application. You also provide details of any application requirements, such as high
availability and scalability, and if you require a backend database.
The PaaS Service then provisions all the necessary infrastructure using the information
provided by automated scripts. It provides an environment to host and support your
application and manages its deployment and lifecycle.
With this service model, you can also easily manage your application's lifecycle and define
different deployment strategies and processes for managing upgrades to the application code.
Most PaaS solutions, such as those offered by AWS, like AWS Elastic Beanstalk, also allow you
to decide how the underlying resources should be configured. For example, if your application
requires high availability, the service will provision the necessary load balancers and deploy
virtual servers across multiple availability zones.
Ultimately, the provider is responsible for configuring and managing the underlying
infrastructure components, including virtual machines, storage, network configurations, and
databases, reducing your overall burden and allowing you to focus more on your application
layer.
For example, you can use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to deploy a complete three-tier application
architecture comprising a load balancer, front and backend compute layers, and a database

Software as a Service
Software as a Service (SaaS) is a cloud idx_69421459 computing idx_8baa2bcd model that delivers a complete end-to-end
software application, usually over the Internet. Hosting and managing any hardware or
infrastructure component is unnecessary since you will not need to install the software locally
in your environment. Most SaaS products are also accessible using a standard browser
interface, although some offer fully functional client desktop applications.
For example, Microsoft Office 365 is a SaaS offering that enables you to access office
productivity tools via the internet. One such tool is Microsoft Exchange, which provides email,
calendar, and task services. You can access your email mailbox account directly on the Office
365 portal over the Internet using the online version of Microsoft Outlook, or install a desktop
edition of the Outlook software to send and receive emails. Microsoft Outlook is the client
software that connects to the server component of Microsoft Exchange.
The important distinction between hosting Exchange on premises and Office 365 is that you do
not need to run your copy of Microsoft Exchange. You do not have to deploy your Exchange
servers or worry about patching them or updating and upgrading the Exchange software when
newer versions are released.
But while SaaS-based solutions remove much of the infrastructure provisioning and
management from the customer to the vendor, certain applications may require end-user
configuration for which you may idx_163c1d13 need to hire subject matter experts (SMEs) who can
configure the product. For example, with Microsoft Exchange, you will still need to set up your
company Exchange idx_0924a01d account and domain names, necessary DNS idx_60498731 records, set up users, groups,
and mailboxes, and define specific security rules and permissions. These tasks would require
you to either have in-house expertise or outsource the configuration and support of the service
to a third party.

enriching digital content. In contrast, Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence tool

In the case of our fictitious client, Belly Brew Co. Limited, a new customer-facing website that
will promote its products and engage with the public must be built, designed, and deployed.
This website can be hosted on an IaaS, PaaS, or even SaaS platform—AWS can offer both IaaS
and PaaS solutions. For a SaaS-based solution, Belly Brew Co. Limited could consider using a
fully managed web hosting platform offering website-building services like WordPress.
Choosing a suitable model depends on your business requirements and whether you are
building an in-house solution or can idx_ff8263a8 subscribe to an off-the-shelf (OTS) product that fulfills
your requirements. For in-house applications, you can opt for an IaaS model or a PaaS solution,
though the latter would have some restrictions. For example, legacy systems may need to be
refactored or re-architected since many PaaS solutions would support only modern languages
and libraries.
SaaS-based idx_9055f113 solutions idx_9565852a take away much of the overhead in managing underlying infrastructure
and the application lifecycle. You don't need to worry about designing, building, and deploying
updates, releases, and bug fixes. This is the vendor's responsibility. However, at the same time,
you do lose the flexibility in how that lifecycle is managed.
While IaaS gives you the flexibility to custom-design and build your underlying infrastructure
that will host your application, it also means that you will need to employ the necessary
expertise to correctly configure, support, and manage that infrastructure, as well as incur the
required costs associated with it. The following table in Figure 2.5 summarizes each cloud

After understanding how responsibility is shared across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, it is equally
important to consider where these cloud environments are hosted. This brings us to cloud
deployment models idx_fd94366c and the advantages and trade-offs each idx_e7bc352d model presents. In the next
section, you will learn more about cloud deployment models, which examine where the
environment's infrastructure is located and its key advantages and disadvantages.
Choosing cloud deployment models
Businesses have idx_1ed981d1 different requirements for hosting and managing their IT resources,
applications, and workloads. Some applications are highly sensitive to latency issues caused by
wide-area networks and must operate as closely as possible to other services or end users. At
the same time, certain businesses must host all their IT services and resources in-house due to
strict compliance and regulatory requirements. Yet another scenario could be that a business
would need to host certain resources on-premises and others in the cloud due to technical
requirements and/or cost control.
Businesses can choose between three primary cloud deployment models (private, public, and
hybrid) for cloud idx_f2efa8af computing deployment. These three deployment models are discussed next.
25 What Is Cloud Computing?
Private cloud
This configuration idx_8cc1be25 involves using virtualization idx_15331088 solutions and software management tools to
deliver self-service capabilities in resource provisioning, configuration, and management. Like
normal cloud environments, end users can define and create resources from the available
infrastructure to fulfill application requirements. The key difference here is that this cloud
environment is usually designed for only internal use by an organization and not external
customers. While this is much like a traditional on-premises environment, resource
management software and self-service modeling are designed to increase the utilization of
available resources and remove excessive administrative burdens.
Private cloud environments lack many features and the economies of scale that are often
attributed to public cloud due to the investment made in the latter by dedicated cloud vendors
such as AWS, Microsoft, and Google. Finally, building a private cloud solution would incur a
sizable capital investment upfront, which is not ideal for many businesses. Nevertheless, some
organizations would still need to host their applications within a private cloud environment
for reasons such as regulatory laws or national security. Another technical reason would be the
requirement for extremely low-latency connectivity.
Public cloud
A public cloud idx_e7d46691 provider, such as idx_55ea9418 AWS, offers access to an extensive range of IT technologies and

services that end customers and partners can use to build solutions and host applications
using a pay-as-you-go model. These providers enable you to design, build, and deploy your
application natively in the cloud and facilitate migrating applications on-premises to the cloud
through various tools and processes. The biggest advantage to using a public cloud service is
that you do not need to procure expensive hardware and can move away from a CAPEX mode
of investment in IT to an OPEX one.
Another key advantage is that cloud providers design and build innovative solutions that are
accessible at affordable prices, leveraging economies of scale due to adoption by a large pool of
customers. Cloud providers also offer access to globally located data center facilities, enabling
you to build highly available solutions, access global markets, and fulfill disaster recovery
strategies, enhancing global customer experience. These features would likely be cost-
prohibitive for most companies if they only adopted traditional on-premises IT services. Small
retail businesses, for example, can benefit from cloud computing by efficiently deploying their
applications across the idx_478cc1a1 globe without having idx_f17b5135 to procure real estate and expensive hardware in
multiple regions, giving them access to a wider customer base.

Hybrid cloud
Hybrid cloud environments idx_5fc2f5ef are a design pattern idx_fc11942d that bridges private and public clouds. Most
companies will find themselves in this configuration simply because, traditionally, they may
have built on an on-premises environment and are now looking to offload a portion of their IT
services to the public cloud. Another reason for hybrid deployments is that certain business
application components must reside on premises due to network bandwidth, latency issues, or
compliance and regulatory laws. Hybrid cloud environments usually involve designing
network and application connectivity between on-premises systems and the public cloud
account.
Companies expanding their IT footprint generally try to identify public cloud options. This
avoids CAPEX expenditure and grants access to cutting-edge technologies and services
through a pay-as-you-go model.
With these deployment models in mind, we can now look more closely at why businesses
adopt cloud computing in idx_4311a261 the first place and how those idx_fbc9cc4d advantages can help Belly Brew Co.
Limited become more agile and competitive.
Applying the six advantages of cloud computing
The cloud offers idx_8aeff6bf several benefits to businesses of all sizes, from new startups to well-
established multinational companies. In this section, we review the six advantages of cloud
computing:
Trade fixed expenses for variable expenses: Traditional IT involves procuring
expensive hardware and building in-house or co-located data center facilities to host
and support your application portfolio. With the cloud, all hardware infrastructure
components are procured and managed by the cloud vendor, leaving you to provision
and consume virtualized IT resources such as virtual machines, storage volumes, and
network services on a pay-as-you-consume model. Belly Brew Co. Limited can rapidly
embark on its cloud journey, paying only for the resources it uses without worrying
about purchasing any physical hardware.
Benefit from massive economies of scale: Cloud providers like AWS serve thousands
of customers across the globe, enabling them to architect, build, and deliver services at
much lower costs, all thanks to the concept of economies of scale. If Belly Brew Co.
Limited were to build its own in-house analytical tools, manage releases, bug fixes, and
support, the costs associated would be much greater than if it used managed offerings
from AWS.

Stop guessing capacity: Traditional on-premises IT infrastructure design and build
patterns often resulted in companies adopting a 'peak load provisioning' model.
Because it is usually difficult to predict demand and capacity requirements, many
businesses would spend extra to ensure they have additional capacity to handle peak

low usage, wasting resources and money.
Many providers, such as AWS, offer auto-scaling services that enable businesses to
provision resources when required and just as quickly terminate them when demand
drops, resulting in better cost management. Using auto-scaling services, Belly Brew Co.
Limited could provision website application servers that would scale out when traffic
to the website increases and scale back in when traffic drops, ensuring a cost-
optimized architecture.
Increased speed and agility: With traditional IT, you would have to wait for long lead
times to deliver physical hardware, which must be installed and configured. This
results in developers having to wait weeks or even months before they can get started
on projects. With cloud computing, you can provision new resources such as servers,
storage volumes, and network resources in seconds. The latter enables you to build a
range of environments to cater to development, testing, and production quickly. Belly
Brew Co. Limited can access cloud computing services to spin up the necessary
infrastructure resources to host their new customer-facing website in minutes, all with
high availability, scalability, and fault tolerance.
Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers: Cloud computing
enables businesses idx_e2394ae4 to focus on their core products and services and the applications
that differentiate them from the competition. There is no need to focus on building,
designing, and investing in the underlying infrastructure, enabling businesses to direct
their precious capital to more important matters, such as designing better products
and solutions or sales and marketing. With cloud computing, the company can
consume cloud IT services and resources to build applications that enable it to better
engage with its customers and ensure quality, on-time products, rather than focus time
and money on data center activities.
Go global in minutes: Cloud providers like AWS offer access to multiple global data
centers across multiple regions. You can deploy your applications across these regions
to ensure global reach over a low-latency network connection. Attempting to build a
global presence in this manner is often cost-prohibitive for many organizations, had it
not been for cloud computing.

traditional on-premises environments. Belly Brew Co. Limited can benefit from moving its
workloads to the cloud, enabling it to design, build, and deploy solutions more quickly and at a
more manageable pay-as-you-go price. Belly Brew Co. Limited's Chief Finance Officer (CFO)
does not need to idx_b41ef8c6 commit large amounts of capital to hardware procurement and can still
benefit from cutting-edge idx_60ce21d3 technologies that can deploy applications that are accessible
globally. Belly Brew Co. Limited can become more agile and deliver new innovative solutions
for both its end customers and internal stakeholders.
Summary
This chapter examines the world of cloud computing at a high level. You learned about how
traditional IT services have evolved into cloud computing thanks to the invention of
virtualization technologies. Understanding the various cloud computing and delivery models
with their features and specific use cases is critical for the exam since knowing which model is
appropriate for particular use cases will be tested.
In practical terms, you will find that many companies have a hybrid cloud solution since the
need to host infrastructure and data on-premises continues to be a requirement across various
industries due to either compliance and regulatory requirements or simply because of latency-
related issues. AWS offers many services to help build hybrid cloud environments across
compute, storage, networking, and security foundations, such as authentication and
authorization processes.
For most small to medium enterprises, looking after infrastructure, whether on-premises or in
the cloud, is costly and incurs additional management overhead. This directs precious
resources toward activities the business would rather not have to deal with. Building
architectural solutions using PaaS and SaaS services removes much of the underlying heavy
lifting associated with IaaS architectures. The goal of a cloud practitioner, then, should be to
help businesses focus on their core products and services and, where possible, pass this heavy
lifting on to AWS. Finally, you learned about the six advantages of cloud computing and how
Belly Brew Co. Limited can benefit by moving its workloads to the cloud.
In the next chapter, we introduce you to the largest cloud provider, Amazon Web Services
(AWS), and its global infrastructure.

Exploring the AWS Global Infrastructure
The AWS Global Infrastructure idx_53ce04e7 comprises several strategically placed data center facilities
across the globe through which over 200 services are offered to its customers. AWS serves
customers from almost every industry, ranging in size from small startups to giant
conglomerates. Its global infrastructure architecture must provide customers with a scalable
and secure infrastructure that offers high availability and durability.
The design of this global infrastructure must fulfill a wide range of use cases. These include
customers who need to deploy applications closer to their end consumers, who may be in
different parts of the world. These customers require single-millisecond latency connections to
their applications or customers who must ensure that they fulfill data residency requirements
by ensuring that data is stored within a particular geographical border.
These use cases vary drastically. For example, the infrastructure components and design
architectures required by Netflix will differ from those of a small startup that delivers services
to a local government organization.
To cater to this widely differentiated customer base while fulfilling regulatory, compliance, and
legal guidelines, AWS has built a global infrastructure comprising different data center design
patterns and required hardware components. This also includes making strategic decisions on
where to buy and lease real estate space and how to use the vast collection of infrastructure
hardware.
The following sections cover the various components of the AWS Global Infrastructure.
Regions
AWS Regions are geographical locations that host one or more data center facilities. You can
think of a data center facility as a idx_ecf393a8 physical building that houses a range of infrastructure
components such as computing, network, and storage services. A region is a strategically
defined geographical area where AWS offers infrastructure, platform, and software services.
These regions are strategically chosen to ensure low-latency access to customers based in and
around that region. Figure 3.1 is an image of the Regions currently deployed by AWS at the time
of writing this book.

The grey dots represent regions that are currently live, and the black ones are regions that will
soon be available to AWS customers. A few more regions may be available by the time this book

For example, AWS has a London region designed for UK-based customers with low-latency
connectivity. However, as shown in Figure 3.2, customers in Northern Ireland may find that the
Dublin region offers idx_9a3f3e4d lower latency. This is simply because the physical distance from Northern

Another reason for having multiple regions is to enable customers to fulfill data residency laws
and regulatory requirements. This is because AWS will never replicate or move any data hosted
in one region to another region. Since each region has its collection of infrastructure services,
such as computing, network, and storage, which are isolated and separated from other regions,
customers can rest assured that any data they host in one region will remain in that region
unless, of course, the customer copies that data to another region.
37 Introduction to AWS and the Global Infrastructure
So, some customers in the idx_cb334e75 UK who are bound by these data sovereignty laws will be able to
ensure that they fulfill those requirements by hosting their applications and data only in the
London region. Taking this concept one step further, some customers in Northern Ireland may
have no choice but to host their applications in the London region because they are bound by
UK laws rather than the European Union (EU) or Irish laws. Those customers would not be
able to use the services in the Dublin region, even though the Dublin region would offer lower
latency.
Regions are further subdivided into availability zones. These are a collection of one or more
data center facilities in large metropolitan areas within a geographical region, such as a
country. These availability zones enable AWS to offer redundancy and high availability, which
are discussed next.
Availability zones
Each region is subdivided into at least two distinct availability zones (AZs). Most regions have
at least three availability zones, and some have even more. You can think of availability zones
as metropolitan areas within which the regional data center facilities are physically located.
Each AZ hosts its collection of compute, storage, and network services. These AZs are up to
60 miles or just under 100 kilometers from each other. This design reduces the possibility of all
zones being affected by common power outages, fires, floods, or other disasters.
The London region has three availability zones. Each region has a designation code, and an
extension of that code represents the availability zone names in that region. For example, the
region code for the London region is eu ‑ west ‑ 2. Similarly, the region code for the North
Virginia region is us ‑ east ‑ 1. The three availability zones within the London region are
eu ‑ west ‑ 2a, eu ‑ west ‑ 2b, and eu ‑ west ‑ 2c.
For some services, you can choose which availability zone to place your resources in. For
example, when you deploy web applications and websites on AWS, they must run on some
compute resource, such as a virtual server. A virtual server is a software-based representation

of a physical computer that allows users to run operating systems and applications on a
remote server, and it handles multiple requests for the service it offers. For example, a
WordPress application on a server will answer visitor requests to view blog articles it hosts.
One such compute service on AWS is the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) service,
which enables customers to host virtual servers (EC2 instances) in the cloud.
When deploying this virtual server or EC2 instance, you must select the availability zone to
deploy it in, as depicted in Figure 3.3.

You also have the option to select ' No preference ', as displayed in the screenshot, if you want
AWS to choose an availability zone for you. In this example, a subnet in availability zone
eu ‑ west ‑ 2b is being selected for the EC2 instance. A subnet represents a subset of the network
range of the main network, known as a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). These subnets are also
known as sub-networks, meaning they are a smaller portion of the main network, specifically
the VPC. VPCs and Subnets allow you to create private networks in the cloud, within which you
host your resources, such as EC2 instances. A VPC spans the entire region, whereas a subnet,
which is a subset range of that VPC, spans a single availability zone. VPCs and Subnets are
discussed in more detail in Chapter 7.
In most cases, you would like to host your applications across multiple virtual servers. As a best
practice, you must spread those servers across multiple availability zones in a region. This
ensures that if one availability zone suffers an outage, your application running on the other
virtual servers in the different availability zones continues to serve customers.
Interestingly, the availability zone names mentioned earlier are not the actual physical names/
IDs of the zones. AWS will randomly map the availability zone names you reference to different
physical zones, which changes from one AWS account to the next. Look at Figure 3.4, which
lists the availability zones in the North Virginia region for two separate AWS accounts:
39 Introduction to AWS and the Global Infrastructure
Figure 3.4: Availability zone names mapped to physical IDs of the zones
Notice that the Development Account availability zone us ‑ east ‑ 1a (part of the us ‑ east ‑ 1 or
North Virginia region) is mapped to the physical ID use1 ‑ az2, whereas the Production Account
is mapped to use1 ‑ az1.
This is a crucial behind-the-scenes configuration feature because it ensures even distribution
of resources across all availability zones, reducing the load on infrastructure services within a
single zone. Consider an example where thousands of customers each have a single EC2
instance in the us ‑ east ‑ 1 region. The majority will choose the us ‑ east ‑ 1a availability zone
simply because it's at the top of the list. However, this would mean that the overall load of
servers running in us ‑ east ‑ 1a will be drastically higher when compared to the other zones. By
randomly assigning the availability zone names to different physical zones in the region, you
get a more even distribution of resources and better performance overall.
When you deploy an EC2 instance to host your website, you must choose a region and a
specific availability zone in that region to host the instance. Furthermore, you must configure a

private network in the AWS account that defines the IP Address boundary within which to host
that instance. This requires you to specify a subnet (or a sub-network) that is tied to a given
availability zone.
As per Figure 3.5, the Belly Brew Co. website is hosted on an EC2 instance running the Linux
operating system in a public subnet in the eu ‑ west ‑ 2a availability zone of the London region.

This is a simple solution, but it has some security risks. Specifically, deploying a production
web application in the public subnet is not recommended. Figure 3.6, later in this chapter,
shows an alternative design where the EC2 instances are deployed in the private subnet.
A subnet is a network idx_ca8dead8 segment that defines an Internet Protocol (IP) address block of a larger
network. This more extensive idx_57c37e4f network is called a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) on AWS, as
illustrated in Figure 3.5. Customers can create isolated networks in their AWS account in the
cloud, each hosting a different application stack to ensure isolation and separation. Within
each VPC, you will have one or more subnets. So, for example, you can have one subnet host
your application and another host your backend database. This further allows you to separate
workloads that belong to an application stack.
Servers and other network devices require an IP address to communicate with each other.
Devices that belong to the same subnet can usually communicate with each other by default
because they are allocated private IP addresses from the same IP block range.
This is like your home network, comprising desktop computers, laptops, tablets, phones, and
printers. Enabling inbound access to these devices would require you to create firewall rules on
your home router/modem so that you can publish services such as your website on the
Internet.
41 Introduction to AWS and the Global Infrastructure
In the same way, you can create firewall rules for your VPC, enabling users on the Internet to
access your website from the Internet, as depicted in Figure 3.4. Don't worry if this seems a bit
complicated right now, as VPCs, subnets, and firewall rules are discussed in detail in Chapter 7.
The critical thing to remember is that, even though availability zones are isolated, they are
close enough to enable synchronous replication with single-digit millisecond latency.
Synchronous replication is where data is copied to another system, like a backup or secondary
system, at the same time it is written to the main system. The opposite of synchronous is
asynchronous, which is where data is first committed to the main system and then copied to
the backup or secondary system.
When designing your application architecture, this allows you to distribute your workloads
across multiple availability zones while ensuring low-latency connectivity between them.
Using this concept, you can ensure your application is built for high availability. High
Availability ensures that redundant systems or components are in place so that if one fails,
others can take over to keep the application running without interruption. As well as building

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 40
chunks.content:
for high availability, you should design your applications to be fault-tolerant. This is where a
system is designed to keep working even if some parts fail.
Figure 3.6 depicts a VPC with two private subnets – one in AZ eu ‑ west ‑ 2a and the other in
eu ‑ west ‑ 2b. The decision to move the EC2 instances hosting the Belly Brew website into the
private subnets, unlike the public subnets in Figure 3.5, is to increase the security posture of the
architecture. This is discussed in detail in Chapter 7.
For now, what you will notice in this architecture is that users on the Internet can still access
the Belly Brew website running on an EC2 instance in a subnet located in the eu ‑ west ‑ 2a AZ,
even if connectivity to the instance in eu ‑ west ‑ 2b is severed due to some issue, such as a
complete power outage. This is possible thanks to an application load balancer (ALB) that
distributes incoming requests across healthy instances in multiple availability zones and
subnets.

Figure 3.6: Application architecture built for high availability
By using AZs, you enable customers to build highly available and redundant application
architectures. In the case of Belly Brew Co Limited, using two EC2 instances to host your
website, where the EC2 instances are placed across two AZs, increases high availability and
redundancy. The last thing Belly Brew wants is for customers to navigate to their website only
to see an error message. You can take this one step further by distributing copies of your
application across multiple regions. This can ensure low-latency access for your users
worldwide, or if you need to adhere to different laws and regulations.
Access to multiple regions and the ability to distribute your application across these regions
also facilitate global redundancy in the case of a regional outage.
An important consideration for the AWS Cloud Practitioner exam is the differences between
services that are regional-based and those that are global. Most services allow you to create
resources based on regional sources. This will enable you to fulfill any compliance and
regulatory requirements, such as ensuring data resides in a specific region. Some services are,
however, global, and the following sub-section provides a quick overview of these.
Global vs. regional vs. zonal services
Most AWS services require you to specify a region within which you can create resources for
that service. For example, when you create an Amazon S3 bucket, which is used to store data in
the cloud, you must first specify the region in which the bucket must be created. The data then
43 Introduction to AWS and the Global Infrastructure
resides in that region where the bucket has been made. In most cases, this also addresses data
residency concerns and the fulfillment of any regulatory and compliance laws.
Some services require that you specify the Availability Zone within which you create a related
resource. This is particularly true for EC2 instances (virtual servers you deploy in the cloud)
and Amazon RDS instances (relational database instances).
Yet again, there are other global services. You do not need to specify the region in which you
deploy a resource related to that service. This ensures that the resources you create within your
AWS account are unique globally.
For example, with Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), you can create IAM users that
represent your colleagues who may need access to services and permissions to perform job
functions in your AWS account. Each IAM user you create is unique in your AWS account
globally and capable of accessing services and resources across all regions and availability
zones as long as necessary permissions have been granted to that user.
While regions and availability zones form a substantial part of the AWS Global Infrastructure,

Edge Locations are another component that enables customers to cater to a more global
customer base efficiently. This infrastructure component is discussed next.
Edge locations and regional edge caches
In addition to regions idx_7af7b3de and availability zones, the AWS Global Infrastructure idx_3019b88d comprises a
globally distributed point of presence (POP) network. This network includes physical
infrastructure components idx_e794d8b9 called edge locations idx_fa6e4c5e and regional edge caches.
Multiple edge locations and regional edge caches are strategically placed across the globe in
many countries and enable direct connection into AWS regions through its backbone high-
speed network. One of the primary use cases of this network of edge locations and regional
edge caches is that they offer content idx_c28bc146 caching services that enable customers to reduce latency
when uploading and downloading data from AWS.
You access this network via several services, including Amazon CloudFront (discussed in

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 11) and Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration (discussed in Chapter 6).
chunks.content:
Chapter 11) and Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration (discussed in Chapter 6).
Consider the use case of the Amazon CloudFront service. Assume you are hosting a website
that distributes product training videos, each about 1GB in size, from a region such as North
Virginia (us ‑ east ‑ 1). Suppose you have a global customer base trying to access the training
content. Customers in Australia may experience slower download speeds than those in North
America.
To help elevate this poor performance, Amazon CloudFront enables access to required content
via the AWS backbone network of edge locations comprising high-speed links. Furthermore,

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio

that content is cached locally at an edge location closer to the end consumer, as depicted in the
following diagram in Figure 3.7.
Figure 3.7: AWS CloudFront utilizing AWS POPs to distribute content
In this example, customers based in idx_a5d4fb26 Australia can retrieve the content from the cache hosted in
locations such as Sydney, Brisbane, Perth, and Melbourne. Once the content has been accessed
at least once, a copy of the training video(s) can be cached locally, ensuring low-latency access
to that data.
Regional edge caches
Caching content at edge locations idx_a792b065 needs to be efficiently managed. After all, there is always
going to be some physical limit to how much data you can cache. To ensure efficient
management of storage services, content that has not been requested for some time will be
purged from these edge locations to make room for more popular content. If such content is
then requested again, it must be retrieved from the origin and downloaded from the Amazon
S3 bucket in North Virginia as per the preceding example.
However, AWS also offers regional edge caches strategically placed to allow less popular
content to reside closer to the end consumer longer. If the content is requested within a set
time frame, called a time to live (TTL), it will be idx_1aa7c51d retrieved from the regional edge cache. It will
then be cached again at edge locations, and this idx_ba6c6b0a approach avoids unnecessary traffic back to
the origin.
45 Introduction to AWS and the Global Infrastructure
AWS Local Zones
For many organizations, the idx_f3fe5204 existing collection of AWS Regions might idx_eb745abc still cause some latency
issues depending on their application use case. Consider large cities or metropolitan areas
where there is a requirement for specific ultra-low latency access to services running on AWS
—perhaps to cater to applications such as gaming or video broadcasting.
AWS offers additional infrastructure in the form of Local Zones, which are distinct from
regions and availability zones. AWS has created additional data centers within those areas that
make up these local zones. These local zones may not host all services offered by AWS, but may
carry most of the services that customers require in those specific locations. Only customers
within close proximity to a local zone can access services within it.
AWS Wavelength
Yet another component of the AWS idx_79201b2a Global Infrastructure is AWS Wavelength. These
infrastructure facilities are designed to offer low-latency and high-bandwidth connectivity for
idx_4ca12ccd mobile devices and users. Wavelength zones involve deploying AWS compute and storage
services within telecommunication houses offering 5G networks so that application traffic
from 5G devices can reach application servers running at these facilities without leaving the

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 44
chunks.content:
provider's network. This drastically reduces latency and substantially improves application
performance that requires edge-based computing and storage services.
AWS Outposts
Many businesses require proper hybrid idx_f568efe8 solutions that enable them to run idx_519dd915 applications locally
within their data centers or on-premises environments with access to cloud services. AWS
Outposts is a fully-fledged infrastructure offering from AWS that enables you to host physical
equipment and run several AWS services locally within your on-premises locations.
The core of this infrastructure offering comprises physical servers ranging from 1U and 2U form
factors to 42U. The " U " stands for rack unit, a standard idx_fa7a259b unit of measurement used to describe
the height of servers and idx_757af1ea other equipment that fit into a rack. 1U is 1.75 inches (4.45 cm) in
height. Contained within these racks are host machines, switches, and patch panels that can
offer all the compute, storage, and network services locally. The service also connects back up
to AWS for seamless management of those services and resources using the same AWS tools
you already know. The benefits idx_cb5cd609 of the AWS Outposts offering include low-latency access to on-
premises systems, local data processing, data residency, and application migration with local
system interdependencies.
Regardless of which components of the AWS global infrastructure you must use to host your
application solution, you must first create an AWS account to access AWS services and
provision the required resources. An AWS account is essentially a resource container – a

mechanism to access AWS services securely. AWS accounts are isolated by default from one
another – this is why multiple customers can access the same set of services you need on AWS.
Still, those other customers will not have any visibility into the resources you provision in your
AWS account.
Your AWS account will give you direct access to all regions and availability zones, though you
may need to request access for some regions depending on which country your business is
hosted in. You will learn more about how to create your first AWS account in Chapter 4. As part
of creating your AWS account, you must also select a support plan, which will be discussed in
the next section.
Comparing AWS support plans
You must select a support plan when idx_eb4b6e34 signing up for a Free Tier AWS account. By idx_cd9f79d5 default, the
basic support plan is provided with every AWS account you create and is free of cost. The
other plans, Developer, Business, Enterprise-on-Ramp, and Enterprise, are chargeable.
Understanding the features offered across the various plans is heavily tested in the AWS
Certified Cloud Practitioner exam and is one you must learn.
The basic support plan
The basic support plan offers a base set of customer services but does not come with any
technical support. Key features of this idx_5e6757e5 plan include:
Customer services and access to communities: You can access customer services to
resolve any issues related to your account, such idx_349d82fb as billing and payments, or if you are
having problems signing into your account. The service can be accessed 24/7. In
addition, you have free access to all documentation, whitepapers, and the AWS re:Post
blog website.
AWS Trusted Advisor: This service inspects the resources you deploy and the services
you consume in your AWS account. It is an advisory service that analyzes your
resources against six categories: Cost optimization, Performance, Security, Fault
tolerance, Service limits, and Operational Excellence. The Trusted Advisor service is an
excellent resource for identifying if your resources are configured in alignment with
industry-recommended best practices. Note that the service is not entirely free and is
tied to the support plan that you subscribe to. Customers on the Basic and Developer
support plan get access to a few core checks, whereas customers on the Business,
Enterprise on Ramp, and Enterprise plans get access to all checks across.
AWS Health: This service offers a dashboard that reports on the availability and
accessibility of all AWS services that may directly impact the resources provisioned in

The developer support plan
This support plan is idx_b35fc6d9 designed for organizations running early development and test workloads
on AWS, where some technical support may idx_71b60ac4 be required during standard business hours. In

This support plan is ideal for Belly Brew Co Limited during the development phase of their web
application. This is because it is relatively cheap compared to the other plans, and you get
technical support related to AWS technologies within standard business hours. While you can

AWS. Furthermore, support is only available via web and chat. No telephone support is
available under this plan. Consider upgrading your support plan if you run production-grade

The business support plan
This support plan gives you access to cloud experts 24/7 who can help you resolve technical
issues you may be having with idx_518e88c5 your AWS resources, which you use to host idx_5416ca53 your applications in
the cloud. If your production systems are currently down, you can get a guaranteed response
from a cloud engineer via chat, email, or phone within one hour. You also get access to third-
party software support, documentation, and forums. Given the business size and purpose of
the website you will build on AWS for Belly Brew Co Limited, this plan is ideal for production-

commerce web application, a one-hour response time in the event of production system
outages might be acceptable. As a cloud practitioner, it would be necessary to discuss the
various plans with Belly Brew and provide the pros and cons of each plan, including cost, to
enable the business to make an informed decision.
The enterprise on-ramp support plan
This support plan is designed for idx_93c6ab4b customers with business-critical and idx_394a3fa6 production workloads
where rapid response from experts is paramount. It offers many services on the Enterprise
Plan, such as 24/7 technical support from cloud experts and access to a pool of technical
account managers (TAMs) who can provide consultative guidance for your idx_ccb8532f specific application

This support plan is the créme de la créme that AWS offers its customers. For a higher fee, you

manager (TAM), response to business/mission-critical issues idx_1dde7a6e within 15 minutes, proactive
support in idx_b32f0092 managing billing and cost optimization for your workloads, as well as access to

Summary
In this chapter, you discovered how the AWS Global Infrastructure is designed to help you
build highly available, fault-tolerant, secure, and cost-effective solutions in the cloud. The
AWS Global Infrastructure is designed to help you develop your solutions in a manner that
ensures low-latency connectivity and can fulfill any compliance or regulatory requirements
required by your business on concepts such as data privacy and data residency. Understanding
the fundamental components of the AWS Global Infrastructure will help you build solutions
for your clients by following industry-standard best practices with high performance,
resilience, and security.
Belly Brew Co. Limited is a UK-based company that serves the UK market. In this scenario, you
would want to host its website and other applications within the London region. The London

Depending on the customer base and their locations, the use of Edge locations can also help
cache content closer to end users—but this will depend on the type of content you plan to host
for the Belly Brew website. For example, if you plan to host lots of videos, then using
CloudFront would be ideal.

AWS is a public cloud service provider that caters to a global customer base comprising start-
ups and multi-national organizations, from the Big 4 accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG,
and PwC) to Netflix. Individuals can also access these services for personal projects or merely
to learn about the ecosystem and gain hands-on experience, proving skills to current and
future employers.
Naturally, if customers across most countries can access AWS services and spin up resources,
they would want to ensure very high levels of security so that one customer's resources are not
accessible by another customer unless explicit permissions are granted. This chapter discusses
the concept of an AWS account, which allows the separation and isolation of resources that
belong to one customer from another.
With AWS, you can also create multiple accounts. There are several use cases for this, the most
common being separating different workload environments such as development, testing, and
production. However, with multiple accounts comes the overhead of additional management
and administration, so the primary reason behind the AWS Organizations service is as a means
to centrally manage these accounts from a security perspective and optimize costs. This
chapter reviews the service's key fundamentals and showcases its core features.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:
Understanding AWS accounts
Architecting a multi-account strategy for your business

Managing multiple AWS accounts with AWS Organizations
Using AWS Control Tower for multi-account governance
In addition to security concepts related to protecting and managing your AWS account(s), this
chapter also aligns with the exam Task Statement 4.2: Understand resources for billing, budget, and
cost management, with a particular focus on AWS Organizations consolidated billing and
allocation of costs in Domain 4: Billing, Pricing, and Support.
Understanding AWS accounts
An AWS account is a container for your AWS resources, where you can create, manage, and
control access to the resources you provision. The account acts as an isolated boundary
between other accounts you own and those of different customers. It also handles
administrative functions such as access management and billing.
When you create an AWS account, you idx_c570e001 have access to the vast array of AWS services from
which you can launch and manage resources – these include computing services, networks,
storage, and databases that you need to host your applications. Each account is tied to a billing
method, and any resources launched incur charges based on AWS pricing models. Each
account also has a Root User who owns the account and has the maximum privileges to access

You can start using AWS by creating a free plan account, as you will see in the next section.
The AWS free tier account
Getting started with AWS is easy. All you need to do is set up a free plan account. AWS recently
changed its free tier offering, which means, unlike the previous 12-month free tier offer with
specific free thresholds across different services, you are now allocated $100 worth of AWS
credits at sign-up to use for your idx_65178506 experimentation and learning efforts. A further $100 worth of
credits is offered if you complete a set of five tasks using the AWS management console. Free
plan accounts are designed for learning and experimentation and run for a maximum of six
months. After six months, you must either convert the account to a paid plan account or AWS
will close it down.
A credit or debit card is required to set up the account, but you are only charged if you exhaust
your free credits. Another important point to note is that certain services are not available in
the free plan account, and enabling or using those services will automatically exhaust your
credits and convert your account into a paid plan account. For example, the AWS Organization
service, designed to help you centrally manage multi-account environments, is not available
under the free plan offering.

Depending on your industry, a single account with numerous applications and environments

Isolation between applications and workloads: You can isolate applications from

isolate certain accounts entirely, if required, and allow access from resources in
different accounts.

designate specific accounts to perform and host audit and security information of other

strategy, you have idx_7147a2ca an exact duplicate environment, ideally running in a different region. In the

Organizational units
You can create Organizational units (OUs) to manage idx_13a4b0c3 these accounts effectively within
similar configurations. An OU is a logical group of one or more AWS accounts that share a
common function—environmental, departmental, or any other grouping strategy you may
wish to adopt. When deciding how to structure idx_bb4889b4 your AWS Organizations service, you must
adopt a functional approach, ensuring that you fulfill specific security requirements rather
than simply creating accounts based on your organization's hierarchy. Many businesses will
have multiple AWS accounts that share similar workload types, such as requiring separate
environments for development, UAT, and production. This would result in creating groups of
accounts that share similar security requirements. For example, the security requirements for
production accounts will differ from those for development accounts.
OUs can also be nested, which enables smaller units of management. For example, you can
create OUs for your Workloads (applications) and then make two nested OUs to divide
production workloads from pre-production.

While separating accounts into various OUs can help isolate workload types, a mechanism is

The following section examines the fundamentals of SCPs in more detail.
Securing OUs and accounts with service control policies
AWS Service Control Policies (SCPs) are guardrails idx_4656d871 you can define for your AWS accounts,
restricting what services can be consumed idx_3421f4f2 and what resources can be launched. With SCPs,
you create policy documents using the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format, allowing
you to define granular idx_cbd722bf permissions on actions in your AWS member accounts.
However, SCPs do not directly define users' actions in your AWS accounts. They are guardrails
defining the maximum permissions administrators can grant users and roles in a member
account. Thus, in addition to creating SCPs, you must also define permissions assigned to your
users and applications within an AWS account that align with the SCP. Only then can those
users and applications access approved services and resources. These permissions are granted
using the AWS IAM service or by creating resource-based policies. A diagram illustrating this
concept is depicted in Figure 4.5:

discussed in detail in Chapter 5.
SCPs can be used to restrict specific actions that apply even to the root users of the
individual member accounts. For example, you can prevent a root user of a member

Each AWS account is usually linked to a payment method along with the contact information

Any projects being worked on would need financial approval from the relevant heads and key
stakeholders.
The AWS Organizations services offer the consolidated billing feature to help companies better

transfers all responsibility for expenses incurred and payments made to the management
account. The feature offers a consolidated view of every service used in each account and
itemized invoices per account.

Shared resources across accounts
Many organizations will have shared infrastructure services, which other teams or
departments may need access to. Sharing resources like idx_59603d50 network subnets of a Virtual Private
Cloud (VPC) across member accounts allows idx_0ad34932 owners of those accounts to deploy their
applications in the shared resource. To share idx_8505abdc such resources, you must first enable the
Resource Access Manager (RAM) service in your AWS Organizations. You can then share
resources with all the other accounts or specific accounts contained within one or more OUs.
Some resource types can also be shared with other AWS accounts not part of your organization.
These include the Backup Vault in AWS idx_72fe185b Backup, which is used to securely store and organize
backups created by AWS Backup. Sharing resources can also help optimize costs. For example,

if you need to deploy virtual servers in the idx_35349d85 cloud, you can use the Amazon Elastic Compute
Service (EC2). This service enables you to deploy virtual machines (virtual servers) running
Windows, Linux, or the MacOS operating system. By default, these instances are purchased
using a pay-as-you-go idx_2943a254 model known as on-demand pricing. On-demand pricing is where you
pay for the resource hourly or by the second.
However, you can also idx_1440465c purchase reserved EC2 instances (RI) contracts. This contract is a
commitment to consume a particular virtual machine with specified attributes (CPU, memory,
network capabilities) for one to three years. These reserved instance contracts are available at a
substantial discount compared to the on-demand hourly price. With AWS Organizations, you
can share reserved instances purchased in the management account with other member
accounts of the organization. This means that if you happen to have spare RI capacity
available, these contracts idx_f7e2dd35 can be fully utilized in other member accounts that might need
capacity. Amazon EC2 and Reserved Instances (RIs) are discussed in detail in Chapter 8.
While AWS Organizations and its core features enable you to streamline the management of a
multi-account architecture, you must still make manual decisions and define configuration
items such as OUs, SCPs, and more. Companies with hundreds of AWS accounts will still
perform several tasks to ensure their organizational structure fulfills recommended best
practices and security guidelines. This can all become very complex and time-consuming. AWS
offers another solution to help idx_f0f62669 create and manage your AWS multi-account architecture more
efficiently, using industry-standard best practices and well-architected idx_e9069ddb references. This service
is called AWS Control Tower and is the topic of the next section.

Using AWS Control Tower for multi-account
governance
AWS Control Tower is a fully managed service designed to help you build complex multi-
account architectures idx_1f67f475 using industry-standard best practices. The service uses the AWS
Landing Zone blueprints to create a secure idx_38e390c1 multi-account environment following well-
architected references. These blueprints incorporate governance, data security, and audit
logging capabilities.
AWS Control Tower offers predefined rules comprising preventive, detective, and proactive
guardrails, allowing you to enforce compliance. Preventive guardrails help to avoid policy
violations, while detective guardrails are designed to monitor your member accounts and
notify you when a policy violation occurs. Proactive controls scan your resources before they
are provisioned, ensuring that they are only provisioned if they are compliant with those
controls.
The service also integrates with the AWS Account Factory, allowing you to create new AWS
accounts from the AWS Organization service using a set of pre-configured settings that ensure
consistency, as well as other services, such as the AWS IAM Identity Center (previously known
as AWS Single Sign On, SSO), AWS idx_a5c46766 CloudTrail, and AWS Config, offering auditing and
governance features. Finally, a central dashboard allows you to monitor your multi-account
environment and review all guardrail compliance statuses and governance metrics.
The AWS Control Tower builds on the AWS Organizations service by providing automated
setup, governance, and best practices for multi-account environments. This makes architecting
and deploying a multi-account environment much more effortless.
